name: Bricklin SV-1
hook: An American dreamed up a gull-winged safety sports car, and had it built in New Brunswick, a Canadian province with no car industry at all.
story:
Picture an American salesman with a big idea. Malcolm Bricklin wants a sports car that keeps you safe. Gull-wing doors. A roll-over cage built into the body. Bumpers that shrug off a five-mile-an-hour bump. Not even a cigarette lighter, because he thinks smoking at the wheel is dangerous.

But where do you build it? Not Detroit. He goes to New Brunswick, on Canada's Atlantic coast. A small province that has never made cars. Its premier, Richard Hatfield, wants jobs. So the province puts money in.

A factory opens in Saint John. Most of the workers have never built a car. The body is fibreglass with acrylic on top, coloured right through, so nothing gets painted. But the cold, damp air fights the bond between the layers. Panels get scrapped. The heavy doors lift slowly.

The money runs out. The company goes into receivership, owing the province millions. Fewer than three thousand cars are made.

A flop on paper. But lift those doors at a car show, and watch a crowd form.
description: The Bricklin SV-1 is a two-seat sports car with powered gull-wing doors, built in Saint John, New Brunswick, from 1974 into 1976. American entrepreneur Malcolm Bricklin named it for "safety vehicle". It had a built-in roll-over structure, energy-absorbing bumpers and a body of acrylic bonded to fibreglass, moulded in colour. The 1974 cars used an AMC 360 V8, later cars a Ford 351 Windsor. The New Brunswick government backed the venture and lost its money when the company went into receivership.
